key_insight: The paper reframes interpretability as one component of a model's broader semantics using a formal philosophy-of-science notion, showing that interpretability claims must be situated within an explicit semantic framework. This clarifies what interpretability can and cannot tell us in biomedical deep learning.
problem_solved: Addresses ambiguity and overreach in interpretability claims for deep models in biomedicine by providing a formal structure to distinguish interpretability from other semantic aspects (e.g., representation, mapping to real-world phenomena).
method: Introduce a formal definition of model semantics drawn from philosophy of science to decompose a model's meaning into distinct parts.
Frame interpretability as one semantic component and delineate its relationships to representation, causal/functional mapping, and domain knowledge.
Illustrate the framework with biomedical deep-learning examples to show how misaligned semantics lead to misinterpretation or misuse.
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners a rigorous checklist to make clearer, testable interpretability claims and to better validate model behaviour in high-stakes biomedical settings, improving trust and translation to practice.
visual_elements: Layered schematic of 'model semantics' showing components: interpretability, representation, mapping to phenomena, and domain constraints.
Flowchart comparing a vague interpretability claim vs. one grounded in the semantics framework (inputs, assumptions, measurable links).
Mini case-study panels for 2–3 biomedical examples showing how semantics analysis changes conclusions or validation steps.
Icon-based legend linking model internals (weights/activations) to clinical variables and evidence types (correlation, mechanism, causal inference).
paper_title: Interpretability and implicit model semantics in biomedicine and deep learning
paper_authors: Jonathan Warrell, Michael Gancz, Hussein Mohsen, Prashant Emani, Mark Gerstein
